item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #453
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent weeks have seen significant developments affecting landlords and property investors across England and Wales. From new registration schemes to ongoing court delays, those in the private rental sector may wish to take note of several important changes that could impact their lettings businesses.

Mandatory Landlord Registration Scheme Announced

The government has confirmed details of its forthcoming national landlord database, with the rollout beginning in the West Midlands on 15th December this year. The scheme will expand regionally, with each area having a three-month window for landlords to complete their registrations. Key points include:

  • Registration costs £66 per property, renewable annually
  • Only currently let properties require immediate registration
  • Vacant properties must be registered before marketing begins
  • Fines will apply for non-compliance

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook described the initiative as an important step towards creating a comprehensive private rental sector database that could benefit both tenants and responsible landlords. Property owners may wish to check the official rollout schedule to ensure they meet their local deadline.

Court Delays Reach 20-Year High

Concerns continue to grow over worsening delays in the possession claims process. Recent Ministry of Justice figures reveal the average repossession case now takes up to 27 weeks - the longest waiting period in two decades. Anecdotal evidence suggests some landlords face additional administrative challenges, with one case seeing court documents arrive weeks after the intended possession date.

While overall possession claims have decreased slightly year-on-year, the extended processing times could present cash flow challenges for some landlords. The government has announced plans to transfer rent challenge cases to HMRC's Valuation Office, potentially easing pressure on tribunal services.

Short-Term Let Registration Coming in 2025

From March 2025, operators of short-term holiday lets in England will need to register their properties on a new national database. The scheme will require landlords to provide property details and pay a registration fee, though full pricing details remain forthcoming. Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Secretary Lisa Nandy stated the register aims to help local authorities balance tourism needs with housing availability while strengthening enforcement capabilities.

With multiple new regulatory requirements coming into force, landlords and property investors might consider reviewing their compliance strategies and diaries to prepare for these changes. Staying informed about implementation timelines could help avoid potential penalties and ensure smooth transitions to the new systems.

item.title: Letting agents accused of cashing in with new landlord charges
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Following the implementation of the Renters' Rights Act, some letting agents have reportedly introduced new charges for landlords to cover additional administrative work. Industry bodies warn that these unexpected fees could strain relationships between agents and property investors, whilst others suggest the costs reflect legitimate compliance burdens.

New Fees Emerge Amid Regulatory Changes

The Telegraph has reported cases of letting agents charging separately for services that were previously bundled within standard fees. These include compliance audits, financial statements and paperwork relating to rent increases. The changes come as agents adapt to increased regulatory requirements under the new legislation, which has also reduced traditional income streams like tenancy renewal commissions.

Examples cited include KFH's introduction of a £12+VAT charge for additional financial statements, whilst some agents reportedly levy up to £300 for compliance audits. The British Landlords Association has cautioned landlords to review their agency agreements carefully, noting that whilst increased administration is understandable, "unexpected or questionable add-on fees" may erode trust in the sector.

Mixed Reactions From Industry Voices

Chris Norris of the National Residential Landlords Association suggests some agents may be capitalising on landlords' compliance anxieties: "With significant sanctions for regulatory breaches, many landlords rely heavily on agents to ensure everything is above board – some may see this as an opportunity to introduce additional charges." He acknowledged some landlords might view such practices as "underhand" whilst others accept them as business costs.

Industry data supports these observations, with Goodlord reporting nearly a quarter of landlords have experienced increased agency fees since the reforms. However, letting agents argue the charges reflect genuine additional workloads. Greg Tsuman of Martyn Gerrard lettings commented: "The reforms require more paperwork from both parties. If landlords choose to outsource this compliance work, it's reasonable for agents to charge accordingly."

Navigating the New Fee Landscape

Landlords concerned about changing fee structures might consider:

  • Reviewing agency agreements to understand what services are included
  • Requesting itemised breakdowns of any new charges
  • Comparing service packages across multiple agents
  • Considering whether to handle some compliance tasks directly

As the sector adjusts to the post-reform environment, transparency around fees appears crucial for maintaining positive landlord-agent relationships. Both parties face new administrative challenges, but how these costs are distributed may significantly influence business decisions in the private rental market.

item.title: Flat prices fall as leasehold headaches weigh on market
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent data reveals a growing disparity between house and flat prices across the UK property market. While house values continue their upward trajectory, flats and maisonettes have recorded notable declines – a trend experts attribute partly to mounting leasehold concerns.

Diverging property price trends

Analysis of Land Registry figures by SAM Conveyancing shows average flat prices dropped 2.27% annually to £216,246 as of June 2026. Over a five-year period, these properties have seen values decrease by 1.56%. This contrasts sharply with the performance of houses during the same period:

  • Semi-detached homes rose 3.16% to £285,618
  • Terraced properties increased 2.76% to £240,147
  • Detached homes gained 1.98% to £463,547

Leasehold complexities weigh on demand

Industry observers suggest multiple leasehold-related factors may be contributing to flats' weaker performance. These include rising service charges, ground rent concerns, Building Safety Act compliance issues, and uncertainty around proposed leasehold reforms.

Andrew Boast of SAM Conveyancing notes: "The decline in leasehold values corresponds directly with growing complications for owners and potential buyers. Transactions frequently stall due to complex lease terms, mortgage protection clauses and unresolved cladding liabilities."

Mortgage approvals for flats may be facing additional hurdles, with lenders applying stricter scrutiny to ground rent terms and lease conditions. Market data indicates nearly 90% of leasehold flats remain unsold after six months on the market – significantly longer than freehold properties.

While leasehold issues appear influential, other market forces may also contribute to the price divergence. Changing buyer preferences post-pandemic, regional variations and affordability pressures could all play a role in the shifting dynamics between property types.

For those considering flat purchases, thorough due diligence around lease terms, service charge histories and building safety certifications might prove particularly important in the current climate. Many homeowners appear to be prioritising the relative simplicity of freehold houses amidst these market uncertainties.

item.title: Property laws in England and Wales drift further apart
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

As property and housing laws in England and Wales continue to diverge, solicitors are being issued new guidance to navigate the growing differences. The Law Society of England and Wales has released a practice note to assist legal professionals in determining which country’s rules apply when advising clients. Whilst England and Wales remain a single legal jurisdiction, devolution has led to an increasing number of Wales-specific laws, particularly in the property sector.

Growing Divergence in Property Laws

The differences between English and Welsh property laws are becoming increasingly significant. Areas such as taxation, social housing, and landlord and tenant responsibilities now operate under separate rules in Wales. This divergence means solicitors working across both countries must carefully identify the correct legal framework for their clients. The new guidance aims to provide clarity on these distinctions, helping practitioners deliver accurate advice tailored to the specific jurisdiction.

Implications for Solicitors and Clients

Mark Evans, president of the Law Society, emphasised the importance of understanding these differences. He noted that whilst England and Wales remain a single jurisdiction, the divergence in areas like property and education has real implications for both solicitors and their clients. Evans, who has experience working in a cross-border firm, stressed that this guidance is essential for supporting legal professionals. The practice note aligns with the Law Society’s ‘Distinct, Not Separate’ position, offering solicitors a practical tool to navigate the complexities of devolved laws.

Looking Ahead

Mark Davies, chair of the National Board for Wales, highlighted the significant development of Welsh law since devolution. He underscored the importance of understanding these differences for solicitors working in England, Wales, and cross-border areas. Davies welcomed the new guidance as a step towards clarifying these distinctions and expressed hope for further work to explore specific areas of devolved law in more detail.

As the legal landscapes in England and Wales continue to evolve, this guidance provides a valuable resource for solicitors navigating the complexities of property and housing laws. Homeowners and landlords may wish to seek advice from legal professionals familiar with the specific rules applicable to their location to ensure compliance and clarity.

item.title: Angela Rayner welcomes green light for £2bn regeneration scheme
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has welcomed planning approval for the first phase of York Central, a £2 billion regeneration scheme that promises to transform a 110-acre brownfield site near the city's railway station. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the project as a "fantastic opportunity" to deliver much-needed homes and economic growth in Yorkshire after decades of planning delays.

Key Features of York Central Regeneration

McLaren Regeneration and Arlington Real Estate will lead the first phase of construction, which includes:

  • Over 1,000 new homes with at least 20% designated as affordable housing
  • A new commercial district and hotel development
  • Improved transport links including a western entrance to York station
  • Public squares, parks and enhanced pedestrian/cycle routes

The development area represents over 40% of York's existing city centre footprint, blending modern infrastructure with the historic urban landscape. Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with the first phase completing around 2030.

Economic and Housing Impact

As one of the largest regeneration projects in Northern England, York Central aims to address both housing shortages and regional economic development. The mixed-use scheme combines residential, commercial and leisure spaces to create a sustainable urban quarter.

Homebuyers and renters in York may find the development particularly interesting given its central location and commitment to affordable housing. The project forms part of the government's wider strategy to boost housing supply while revitalising urban areas through public-private partnerships.

This long-awaited approval marks a significant milestone for Yorkshire's property market, potentially offering new opportunities for first-time buyers and investors alike once construction begins. The phased approach allows for careful integration with York's existing infrastructure while delivering modern housing and workspaces.

item.title: Property tribunal cases surge amid Renters’ Rights shake-up
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property-related tribunal cases in England have surged significantly, according to recent data from the Ministry of Justice. The figures, highlighted by property consultancy Savills, reveal a 24% year-on-year increase in cases handled by tribunals in the 12 months to June 2026. This rise is driven by a range of residential property disputes, including rent reviews, leasehold conflicts, enfranchisement claims, and cases under the Housing Act 2004. The sharp uptick in tribunal activity coincides with the implementation of the Renters’ Rights Act, which is reshaping the private rented sector.

Rising Tribunal Cases Reflect Market Changes

The latest tribunal statistics show a particularly steep rise in quarterly figures, with 4,613 cases recorded in Q2 2026 alone—a 56% increase compared to the same period in 2025. This spike is attributed to the ongoing adjustments within the rental market as landlords and tenants navigate the new regulations introduced by the Renters’ Rights Act. Savills predicts that tribunal activity will continue to grow as the legislation becomes more embedded, particularly in relation to rent reviews, which are expected to generate a significant number of cases.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, commented: “As the Renters’ Rights Act beds in, we’d expect to see the number of cases referred to tribunals rise exponentially, particularly concerning rent reviews. Both landlords and the government will be closely monitoring the capacity to process these cases efficiently.”

Implications for Landlords and Government

The surge in tribunal cases raises important concerns for both landlords and policymakers. For buy-to-let landlords, delays in resolving cases could impact their ability to charge reviewed market rents, potentially affecting their rental income. Meanwhile, the government faces challenges in managing the administrative costs associated with processing the rising number of cases. There may also be a need to revisit and refine the regulations to ensure they are functioning as intended.

Cook added: “Landlords will be particularly concerned about delays in implementing market rent reviews. On the other hand, the government will need to balance the administrative burden with the effectiveness of the regulations.”

As the private rented sector continues to adapt to the Renters’ Rights Act, tribunal capacity and case resolution times are likely to remain under scrutiny. Both landlords and tenants may wish to stay informed about their rights and responsibilities under the new legislation to navigate the evolving landscape effectively.

item.title: The Saturday hour when property viewings surge
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research reveals that Saturday morning remains the golden hour for property viewings, with 11am emerging as the peak time for prospective buyers to tour homes. According to data from property software provider Alto, nearly 250,000 viewings commenced during this single weekly timeslot over the past year – accounting for 4.6% of all weekly viewing activity.

The weekend viewing rush

The analysis shows an overwhelming preference for Saturday appointments, with all five busiest viewing slots falling on this day. Following the 11am peak, 10am claims second place, followed by midday, 1pm and 2pm. By contrast, Friday at 4pm represents the most popular weekday viewing time, though volumes remain 45% lower than Saturday's peak periods.

The figures highlight how traditional working hours continue to dominate the property viewing landscape. Some 95% of appointments occur between Monday and Saturday from 9am to 6pm, with just 4.69% taking place on Sundays or after 6pm. Saturday alone generates 11.5 times more viewings than Sunday, suggesting many buyers prefer to keep their weekends free for property hunting.

Cancellation patterns and out-of-hours opportunities

While Saturdays attract the most viewers, they also see higher cancellation rates. The 10am slot records the highest proportion of cancellations at 23%, compared to just 19% for 7pm appointments and Sunday viewings. This pattern suggests some buyers may overcommit to early weekend viewings before changing their plans.

The data reveals significant variations in estate agent availability outside standard hours. Of the 2,228 branches analysed, 10.5% recorded no viewings after 6pm, while 24% didn't book a single Sunday appointment. Where evening viewings do occur, unaccompanied appointments become more common – representing 71% of 7pm viewings compared to just 25% during weekday working hours.

Seasonal differences also emerge, with evening viewings accounting for 3.8% of summer appointments compared to just 2.1% in January. Industry experts suggest that extending availability could help agents capture more business, with some providers now offering automated booking systems to handle out-of-hours enquiries.

For homeowners considering selling, these patterns may influence how they schedule viewings. While weekends remain prime time, the lower cancellation rates and reduced competition during evening slots could make these less conventional times worth considering when arranging property tours.

item.title: Managing agents face growing threat as Right to Manage cases surge
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Leaseholders across England and Wales are increasingly taking control of their buildings through Right to Manage (RTM) schemes, with new research revealing record numbers of resident-led management companies being established. Property management specialists Placekeeper report that 986 RTM companies formed in 2025 – a 79% surge compared to six years prior – with this upward trend continuing through 2026.

Residents taking charge of building management

The latest figures show a striking divergence between RTM activity and broader housing market trends. Whilst annual housing completions fell by 20% between 2019 and 2025, dropping to 170,390 properties, RTM company formations have more than doubled relative to housing stock during the same period. Placekeeper's newly launched RTM Index, which tracks this relationship, jumped from 69 to 155 points over six years.

Meanwhile, traditional management company formations have declined significantly since their 2018 peak of 2,180, falling to just 1,543 last year – the lowest figure in over a decade. This contrasting pattern suggests leaseholders in existing developments are driving the RTM boom, rather than new-build properties coming to market with resident management structures already in place.

A shifting landscape for property management

Industry experts suggest several factors behind this growing preference for resident-controlled management:

  • Heightened awareness of leaseholder rights following high-profile cases
  • Increased scrutiny of service charges and management transparency
  • Changing expectations around communication and value for money

Trevor Adey of Placekeeper Management notes: "The sustained growth in RTM activity, whilst other property management indicators decline, signals a fundamental shift in how leaseholders want their buildings run. Managing agents who fail to meet evolving standards risk losing contracts to resident-led alternatives."

The research draws on Companies House incorporation data and official housing statistics, painting a clear picture of changing governance patterns in leasehold properties between 2010 and 2026. With 578 RTM companies already formed in the first half of 2026, this year looks set to surpass previous records.

For leaseholders considering their options, the RTM process allows qualifying residents to take over building management without needing to prove fault by the current managing agent. However, establishing an RTM company requires careful planning and adherence to strict legal procedures. Those exploring this route might benefit from professional advice to navigate the process effectively.

item.title: Treasury rejects stamp duty break to get downsizers moving
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The Treasury has dismissed calls for a new stamp duty relief aimed at incentivising homeowners to downsize to smaller properties. In a written response to a proposal by Frontdoor founder Joel Hagan, HM Treasury confirmed it has no plans to introduce further Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) exemptions for downsizers. The decision comes amidst growing concerns about the lack of family homes on the market and the challenges faced by older homeowners looking to move.

What Was Proposed?

Hagan’s proposal, dubbed “Rightsizing Relief,” suggested a capped stamp duty exemption for homeowners selling larger properties and purchasing smaller ones. The aim was to encourage downsizing, freeing up larger family homes for growing families. However, the Treasury rejected the idea, arguing that many downsizers already benefit from substantial equity in their existing properties and enjoy Private Residence Relief from Capital Gains Tax when selling their main home.

Additionally, the Treasury pointed out that the stamp duty bill on smaller replacement properties is often relatively modest, sometimes lower than estate agent fees. It also highlighted the importance of SDLT receipts to public finances, with the tax raising approximately £12 billion annually. Introducing another relief, it argued, could impose a significant cost on the Exchequer.

Disputed Financial Assumptions

Hagan disputes the Treasury’s assessment, claiming that his proposal could actually generate a net annual gain of £180 million for the government. His financial model assumes that each downsizing move could unlock around 2.5 further transactions, with half of these occurring regardless of the relief. According to the model, 100,000 rightsizing moves would result in £625 million of foregone stamp duty but generate £805 million through onward transactions and associated activity.

Hagan criticised the Treasury’s static costing, stating, “Stamp duty is a tax on moving. It raises nothing from a house that does not change hands, so any costing that ignores the transactions a relief creates will always produce a large negative number.” He emphasised that downsizing often triggers a chain of property transactions, benefiting multiple buyers and sellers.

Impact on the Property Market

The debate highlights the broader challenges facing the UK property market, particularly the shortage of larger family homes. Encouraging downsizing could help address this issue, but the Treasury’s decision suggests that policymakers are prioritising the stability of public finances over targeted tax reliefs. For homeowners considering downsizing, it may be worth exploring other financial incentives, such as the existing Capital Gains Tax relief, to make the move more affordable.

Whilst the Treasury’s decision may disappoint those advocating for stamp duty breaks, it underscores the complexity of balancing property market dynamics with fiscal responsibility. Homeowners looking to downsize may still find opportunities to reduce costs by carefully planning their property transactions and seeking professional advice.

item.title: BTL landlord crackdown begins as tougher Renters’ Rights penalties bite
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords failing to comply with licensing requirements now face significantly steeper penalties, as demonstrated by a recent case in Bristol where a buy-to-let investor received a £13,090 fine. The sanction comes as local authorities begin wielding enhanced enforcement powers under the Renters' Rights Act, signalling a tougher approach to housing regulation violations.

Bristol case highlights rising penalties

Bristol City Council imposed the substantial civil penalty after discovering a portfolio landlord had been operating a house in multiple occupation (HMO) without the mandatory licence. This marks the first enforcement action under the council's updated Civil Penalty Policy, which considers previous breaches when determining fines. The landlord in question had allegedly managed other unlicensed HMOs in the past, only applying for necessary permissions when investigations began.

Initially set at £17,000, the fine was reduced after the landlord submitted a licence application within fourteen days. Officials noted the property's below-market rent meant no additional surcharge applied, though rents exceeding Local Housing Allowance rates could trigger supplementary penalties of up to £1,309. From May 2026, maximum civil penalties for housing offences will rise to £40,000 under the Renters' Rights Act.

Tenants may reclaim rent payments

Beyond council-imposed fines, landlords risk facing further financial consequences through Rent Repayment Orders. Tenants occupying unlicensed properties can potentially reclaim up to two years' rent through these legal mechanisms. The Bristol case serves as a timely reminder that licensing breaches can trigger multiple layers of financial liability for property investors.

Councillor Barry Parsons, housing committee chair at Bristol City Council, emphasised the policy aims to protect both tenants and responsible landlords: "The vast majority of landlords operate compliantly and needn't worry about these enhanced penalties, which target serious or repeated offenders." The council stressed its commitment to ensuring rental properties meet safety standards while maintaining fairness for landlords who fulfil their legal obligations.

With housing authorities gaining stronger enforcement tools, buy-to-let investors may wish to review their property portfolios to ensure full compliance with licensing requirements. The regulatory landscape continues evolving, making ongoing diligence increasingly important for landlords seeking to avoid substantial financial penalties and reputational damage.

item.title: Estate agency launches AI-powered property search
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Hortons Estate Agents has introduced an artificial intelligence-powered property search tool designed to streamline the home-hunting process. The new feature, called Intelligent Search, allows prospective buyers to find homes, relocation details and local agents using natural language queries rather than traditional filters.

How the AI property search works

The system processes more conversational search terms such as "3-bedroom Victorian houses near good schools in Manchester" rather than requiring specific postcodes. Results are ranked by relevance, with the algorithm considering multiple factors beyond simple location parameters. Homeowners may find this approach particularly useful when researching areas they're less familiar with.

Key features include:

  • Natural language processing for more intuitive searches
  • Combined results showing properties, area information and agent contacts
  • Integration with traditional filters for those who prefer conventional searching

AI's growing role in property transactions

During its one-month beta testing phase, the tool processed over 14,000 searches independently from the agency's standard property search function. Hortons describes this innovation as part of its broader shift towards becoming an "AI-augmented" agency, with plans for further technological developments in the pipeline.

Adam Horton, founder of the self-employed agency platform, explained: "Our aim is twofold - to enhance agent efficiency while improving the experience for buyers and sellers. By automating certain processes, our agents can focus more on the personal aspects of property transactions."

While traditional search filters remain available, this development highlights how machine learning is increasingly shaping the property market. For those considering a move, such tools could prove valuable when beginning their property search, particularly when exploring unfamiliar locations or specific housing requirements.

item.title: Property industry’s 24-hour marathon raises welcome funds for charity
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The property industry recently came together for a unique 24-hour broadcast event that not only provided valuable insights but also raised over £4,375 for charity. The 24-Hour Open House, hosted by consultant Toby Martin, featured 44 back-to-back sessions with 57 industry experts, attracting 354 unique viewers who collectively watched more than 560 hours of content. The event, which took place from 9am on 3 September to 9am the following day, saw a surprising level of engagement, with participants posting 828 comments and even staying active during the early hours of the morning.

Insights and Expertise on Demand

For those who missed the live event, 28 sessions are now available to watch on demand, with more set to be released. The archive features contributions from a diverse range of property and marketing professionals, including Rory Sutherland, vice chairman of Ogilvy, who explored the psychology behind buying decisions. Other notable participants include property market analyst Kate Faulkner, trainer Stephen Brown, LinkedIn consultant John Espirian, and Nudge podcast host Phill Agnew. The sessions cover a wide array of topics, from marketing strategies to industry training, making it a valuable resource for professionals and enthusiasts alike.

Engagement Beyond Expectations

One of the most surprising aspects of the event was the level of audience engagement, particularly during the overnight hours. Martin admitted he had expected to be speaking into a void during the small hours but instead found himself part of what he described as "a very long night in the pub with the entire industry." The event even saw an unexpected appearance from comedian Mark Watson, adding a touch of humour to the proceedings. Requests for access to the recordings began flooding in before the live event had even concluded, highlighting the demand for the valuable content shared during the broadcast.

Access to the on-demand sessions is available in exchange for a donation to Breast Cancer Now and Andy’s Man Club, two charities that make a significant impact both within and beyond the property industry. Thanks to sponsorship from Kotini, all donations go directly to these causes. This initiative ensures that the event continues to raise funds and awareness long after the live broadcast has ended.

The 24-Hour Open House not only showcased the expertise and camaraderie within the property industry but also demonstrated its commitment to supporting important charitable causes. For those looking to gain insights or contribute to these worthy charities, the on-demand sessions offer an excellent opportunity to do both.

item.title: Thousands of tenanted homes up for sale – what estate agents need to know
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals over 8,500 rented properties with tenants in place are currently available for purchase across England, representing 1.8% of all homes on the market. The figures from The Letting Partnership highlight opportunities for landlords seeking immediate rental income, though experts caution about important financial checks required during such transactions.

Regional variations in tenanted property sales

Analysis shows significant regional differences in the availability of tenanted properties for sale. Northern areas dominate the market, with Yorkshire and the Humber having the highest proportion at 5.1% of local listings (1,575 properties). The North West leads in absolute numbers with 2,227 tenanted homes available (4.6% of stock), followed by the North East's 601 properties (4.3%).

Southern regions present a contrasting picture, with London showing just 0.3% of properties marketed with tenants in situ. The South West and South East record slightly higher proportions at 0.7% and 0.9% respectively. These regional variations may reflect different investment patterns and housing market conditions across the country.

Key considerations when purchasing tenanted properties

Purchasing a property with existing tenants offers the advantage of immediate rental income, avoiding void periods. However, prospective buyers and their agents must carefully review several financial aspects:

  • Tenancy deposit protection arrangements and whether these need transferring or re-registering
  • Complete rent payment history to identify any arrears or outstanding balances
  • Apportionment of rent if completion occurs mid-rental period

Financial experts emphasise maintaining a clear audit trail covering deposits, rent payments and any outstanding amounts. The tenancy's financial history transfers with the property, meaning new landlords effectively inherit the existing arrangement with all its obligations and records.

For landlords considering such purchases, thorough due diligence and professional advice could help navigate the specific challenges of tenanted property transactions while capitalising on their potential benefits.

item.title: Rental arrears hit record low – but one in four landlords still affected
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Rental arrears in the UK private lettings market have reached their lowest level on record, according to fresh research from Pegasus Insight. The study reveals that 26% of landlords faced late or missed rent payments over the past year – a significant improvement from the 42% peak recorded in 2020. This marks the sixth consecutive year of declining arrears across the sector.

Portfolio size impacts landlord experiences

While the overall figures show progress, the data highlights stark differences between small-scale and professional landlords. Those managing larger portfolios appear particularly vulnerable, with 66% of landlords owning 11 or more properties experiencing rental arrears. In contrast, only 18% of landlords with one to ten properties reported payment issues.

The research also examined rental voids, which remain more common than payment problems. Some 41% of landlords dealt with vacant periods exceeding seven days, averaging 66 days without rental income. Again, portfolio size played a decisive role – 68% of larger landlords faced voids compared to 35% of smaller operators.

Tenant perspectives reveal ongoing pressures

Complementary research into tenant experiences surveyed 3,000 private renters. While 12% admitted missing a rent payment in the past year, approximately 90% described their rental costs as either manageable or comfortable. However, the study notes that some renters continue making difficult budgeting choices between housing costs and other essentials.

Bethan Cooke, Director at Pegasus Insight, commented: "The reduction in arrears to 26% is certainly positive, especially considering the financial challenges both tenants and landlords have navigated in recent years. But we shouldn't view this as evidence those pressures have fully eased."

Cooke highlighted the ongoing balancing act in the rental market: "Larger landlords remain disproportionately affected by arrears, while void periods still impact two in five property owners. With inflation lingering and operating costs rising, the sector remains finely balanced between affordability and sustainability."

Industry observers suggest these findings may influence landlord strategies regarding tenant selection, rent pricing and portfolio management. As market conditions evolve, both landlords and tenants may wish to stay informed about their rights and responsibilities under current tenancy agreements.

item.title: UK rental market splits as rents fall in key regions
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK rental market presented a varied landscape in August, with regional divergences becoming increasingly pronounced. While average rents declined in London, the South East and Scotland, other regions experienced steady increases, highlighting the uneven pressures faced by tenants across the country.

Regional rent variations

August's figures from Propertymark revealed notable discrepancies between rental markets. The South East led monthly declines with a 1.8% reduction, followed by Scotland (1.2%) and London (0.7%). Conversely, the East Midlands and East of England both saw 0.8% rises, while Wales and Yorkshire and Humberside recorded 0.7% increases. More modest growth occurred in the West Midlands (0.6%) and North West (0.5%).

Despite London's slight monthly decrease, it maintains its position as the nation's most expensive rental market, with average rents standing at £2,467. Propertymark estimates tenants now require £74,010 annual income to secure an average-priced London rental - a 3.3% increase from £71,670 a year earlier.

Affordability challenges persist

Rental affordability remains stretched across multiple regions. Alongside London's increases, Scotland saw required incomes rise 2.1%, while the North East and West Midlands both experienced 1.5% jumps. However, some renters benefited from improved conditions, with Yorkshire and Humberside recording a 3.7% fall in required earnings and the North West seeing a 1.2% decrease.

Kim Lidbury of ARLA Propertymark noted: "These movements reflect the underlying balance between supply and demand, as well as the availability and type of properties coming to market. Where demand continues to outstrip supply, competition places upward pressure on rents."

Industry experts suggest the current market conditions present challenges for both tenants and landlords. With rising operational costs and regulatory changes affecting property owners, renters may wish to research local market trends thoroughly when considering new tenancies. Those in regions experiencing price drops might find slightly improved negotiating positions, though overall affordability remains constrained.

The data underscores the importance of monitoring regional variations when making rental decisions. While some areas show modest relief, the broader picture suggests the rental market continues to present significant affordability challenges across much of the UK.

item.title: Major estate agency group relocates as revenue and profits rise
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The Property Franchise Group (TPFG), one of the UK’s leading property franchising companies, has announced a relocation of its registered office from Bournemouth to Grantham. This move coincides with the release of its latest financial results, which show a notable rise in both revenue and profits for the first half of 2026.

Financial Performance Highlights

TPFG reported a 7% increase in group revenue, reaching £43.3 million for the first half of 2026, up from £40.3 million in the same period the previous year. On a like-for-like basis, revenue grew by 4%. The group’s franchising revenue saw an 8% rise to £24 million, while financial services revenue increased by 10% to £13 million. Licensing revenue remained steady at £6.3 million.

Adjusted pre-tax profit also rose by 7% to £15.5 million, and adjusted EBITDA increased by 3% to £16.2 million. The group managed to reduce its net debt significantly, from £10.9 million to £8.1 million. Additionally, cash generated from operations saw a slight uptick, rising to £13.4 million from £13.2 million. Despite these positive figures, recurring revenue as a percentage of group income dropped marginally from 47% to 46%.

Strategic Moves and Future Plans

The relocation of TPFG’s registered office to Grantham marks a strategic shift for the group. The new address, The Old Court House on London Road, became effective on 9 September. This move follows the acquisitions of SAFS and Meridian, as well as the introduction of AI-enabled products, which the group believes will bolster its platform further.

Gareth Samples, CEO of TPFG, commented on the group’s performance, stating, “Whilst the external environment remains uncertain, our diversified income streams and growing recurring revenue base give us confidence in delivering our plans for the full year.” He also highlighted the group’s commitment to innovation and expansion, which includes leveraging technology to enhance its services.

In line with its financial success, TPFG announced a 10% increase in its interim dividend, raising it to 7.7p per share. The group owns several well-known estate and letting agency brands, including Belvoir and Martin & Co, which continue to perform strongly in the market.

As TPFG looks ahead, its focus remains on sustaining growth and adapting to the evolving property market. With a strong financial foundation and strategic initiatives in place, the group is well-positioned to navigate future challenges and opportunities.

item.title: Housing market steadies but rent rise expectations surge
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market is showing tentative signs of stabilisation, with buyer demand and agreed sales improving in August, according to the latest RICS UK Residential Market Survey. However, the market remains fragile, with ongoing uncertainty around interest rates and broader economic factors continuing to weigh on confidence.

Modest improvements in buyer activity

August saw a fifth consecutive monthly improvement in new buyer enquiries, with the net balance rising to -19%, the least negative reading since January. Agreed sales also strengthened, with the net balance improving to -17%, up from -38% in April. This marks the strongest performance since February, suggesting a gradual recovery in activity.

Looking ahead, expectations for sales over the next three months edged closer to neutral, with the net balance improving to -3% in August. Over the next 12 months, a net balance of +6% of survey respondents anticipate an increase in sales volumes, up from +3% previously. Jeremy Leaf, North London estate agent and former RICS residential chairman, noted that a modest uptick in demand has coincided with holidaymakers returning to the market, though activity remains lower than this time last year.

House prices remain under pressure

While buyer activity has improved slightly, house prices continue to face downward pressure. The headline price balance edged up to -28% in August, from -29% in July, but remains firmly in negative territory. Survey respondents expect prices to fall in the short term, with the 12-month outlook remaining broadly flat.

Regional variations persist, with London recording a more negative price balance than the national average, despite slight improvements from July. In contrast, Northern Ireland continues to buck the trend, with respondents reporting rising prices. The North West of England also showed relative resilience compared to other regions.

Rising rental expectations

Whilst the sales market remains subdued, expectations for rental price increases have surged. Survey respondents anticipate significant upward pressure on rents in the coming months, driven by a combination of strong tenant demand and a lack of available rental properties. This trend could place further strain on renters, particularly in urban areas where demand is highest.

The outlook for the housing market remains uncertain, with factors such as mortgage rates, inflation, and potential tax changes in the Budget likely to influence activity in the coming months. Borrowers and homeowners may wish to stay informed about market developments and seek professional advice to navigate this complex landscape.

As the autumn property market season approaches, sustained activity will depend on whether economic conditions remain stable. For now, the market appears to be moving sideways, with cautious optimism tempered by ongoing challenges.

item.title: Regional deadlines unveiled for new national landlord register
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The government has announced regional rollout dates for England’s new Private Rented Sector Database, revealing when landlords must register their rental properties between 2026 and 2027. The phased introduction begins in the West Midlands, with other regions following monthly until completion in November 2027.

Registration deadlines by region

Landlords with assured or regulated tenancies must register each rental property they own, providing personal details, tenancy information and safety certification. The registration fee stands at £65 per property, renewable annually. Here are the regional deadlines:

  • West Midlands: 14 March 2027
  • East of England: 14 April 2027
  • East Midlands: 14 May 2027
  • South East: 14 June 2027
  • Yorkshire and the Humber: 14 July 2027
  • North West: 14 August 2027
  • North East: 14 September 2027
  • London: 14 October 2027
  • South West: 14 November 2027

Property owners who miss their regional deadline could face financial penalties. The database will require up-to-date gas safety certificates, electrical installation condition reports and Energy Performance Certificate ratings.

Implications for letting agents

While landlords must complete the registration process themselves, letting agents will play a supporting role in the new system. Agents will eventually need to include registration numbers in property listings and may assist landlords with uploading required documentation.

Industry body Propertymark has raised concerns about the registration being landlord-only. Timothy Douglas, their Head of Policy and Campaigns, noted: "Letting agents frequently manage properties on landlords’ behalf, yet can’t register properties directly. This could create administrative bottlenecks as each landlord must register separately."

Agents will however be permitted to upload safety certificates and property details if authorised by the landlord. The phased rollout aims to give all parties time to prepare, though some industry voices suggest a centralised agent registration system might improve efficiency.

Landlords and agents may wish to note their regional deadline well in advance, as the database becomes a mandatory requirement for all private rented properties in England. The government intends the system to improve standards and transparency in the private rental sector.

item.title: Agents warned of major workload from new landlord database
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The government's new Private Rented Sector Database is set to launch regionally as part of the Renters’ Rights Act, requiring landlords to register properties at £65 per year. While industry bodies welcome clarity on timelines, concerns persist about duplicative costs, enforcement effectiveness, and potential gaps in improving rental standards.

Mixed industry response to landlord database

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) acknowledges the benefits of a clear implementation timetable but warns the database risks becoming a superficial landlord directory rather than a robust compliance tool. NRLA chief executive Ben Beadle suggests the system should actively verify property standards and ownership using existing data, rather than relying on landlords to self-report documents.

Industry professionals highlight that many landlords already pay for local licensing schemes collecting similar information. The NRLA urges the government to clarify how these parallel systems will integrate to avoid duplicate costs and administrative burdens. Without proper coordination, compliant landlords might effectively pay twice for providing identical information through different schemes.

Potential enforcement complications

Legal experts caution that overlapping registration regimes could create confusion around enforcement. Property disputes specialists note landlords might theoretically face penalties under both national and local schemes for the same issues. This raises questions about how enforcement priorities will be determined between different authorities.

The current proposal leaves several practical questions unanswered:

  • How local licensing data will integrate with the national system
  • Whether registration fees will replace or supplement existing local charges
  • How councils will utilise the database for targeted enforcement
  • What verification processes will ensure data accuracy

Housing campaigners argue the database should actively drive up standards by making non-compliance harder to conceal, rather than simply creating an address list of rental properties. Some suggest linking registration to mandatory property inspections or existing energy performance certificates to verify living conditions.

Looking ahead

As the rollout progresses, landlords and letting agents may wish to monitor how regional implementations address these concerns. The database's ultimate success may depend on whether it evolves into an intelligent compliance tool or remains a basic registration portal. With the private rented sector playing an increasingly vital role in the UK housing market, getting this balance right could benefit tenants, landlords and local authorities alike.

item.title: Buyer demand jumps as September housing market springs to life
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK housing market has shown signs of renewed vigour as buyer demand surged at the start of September, according to the latest data from Rightmove. The property portal reported a 5% increase in buyer activity during the first week of the month, significantly higher than the average 0.4% rise typically seen over the past five years. This uptick suggests that potential homebuyers returned to the market more swiftly after the summer break, though demand remains 9% lower than the same period last year.

Regional Variations in Buyer Demand

Rightmove’s data highlights that every region across Great Britain experienced an increase in buyer demand during early September. London led the way with a notable 9% rise, followed closely by the South West at 8%. The West Midlands and North East both recorded increases of around 7%, while the East Midlands and South East saw a 6% uplift. Other regions, including the East of England and North West, also saw modest gains. Wales and Scotland, however, experienced more subdued growth, with increases of 3% and 1% respectively.

Factors Influencing the Market

The stronger-than-usual September bounce follows a challenging summer for the housing market, which faced headwinds from economic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, and extreme weather conditions. Whilst the latest figures indicate a promising start to the autumn selling season, it’s worth noting that buyer demand remains below last year’s levels. Property commentators suggest that whilst the increase is encouraging, it may take further weeks to assess whether this trend will sustain and narrow the annual gap.

Colleen Babcock, Rightmove’s property commentator, commented: “It’s positive to see buyers re-engaging with the market as we move into autumn. However, with the month still in its early stages, it’s important to monitor how this momentum develops in the coming weeks.”

For homeowners considering selling, this uptick in demand could present an opportune moment to list their property. Borrowers might also wish to explore mortgage options to capitalise on the renewed activity in the market. As the autumn season progresses, it remains to be seen whether this early September boost will translate into sustained growth across the UK housing market.
